passages.t: ‘How long, O LORD?’, and ‘But I have trusted’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David” (verse 1).

Then four times in two verses comes the same cry. “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?” (verse 1). “How long must I wrestle in my soul, with sorrow in my heart each day? How long will my enemy dominate me?” (verse 2).

Next comes a plea. “Consider me and respond, O LORD my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death” (verse 3). He fears his enemy will say, “I have overcome him” (verse 4).

Then the psalm turns on one small word. “But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation” (verse 5). It ends, “I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me” (verse 6).

Nothing in the psalm says the trouble ended. The turn comes before any rescue is reported.
passages.hearers:
Psalm 13 is one of the shortest laments in the Psalms, yet it has all the steps of one: a complaint to God, a request, and a turn to trust. The book page on the Psalms uses it to show what a lament is.

Two pictures would hit the first hearers hard. God's ‘face’ meant his favour and presence. The priests blessed the people with the words, “may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25). To feel God hide his face was to feel shut out. And to ‘forget’ in Hebrew is not only to stop thinking about someone. It is to stop acting for them. So ‘Will You forget me?’ means ‘Will You leave me without help?’

‘Give light to my eyes’ asks for life and strength. Dull eyes were a sign of a body failing.
passages.later:
The cry ‘How long?’ runs through Scripture. Habakkuk begins, “How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear” (Habakkuk 1:2). In Revelation even the martyrs in heaven cry, “How long, O Lord, holy and true” (Revelation 6:10).

The God who seems to hide is the God who promised, “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5, quoting Deuteronomy 31:6). Psalm 13 is how a believer prays when that promise is hard to feel.
passages.hard:
Does verse 5 mean that if you trust enough, the sorrow will lift by the end of the prayer? No. The psalm says nothing about how long the nights lasted, and Psalm 88 never turns at all. Read the note on Psalm 6 on this.

If ‘sorrow in my heart each day’ (verse 2) is your life now, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Psalm 13 gives you permission to ask God ‘How long?’ four times over. That is not a lack of faith. It is faith arguing with God because it still believes he is there.

Notice what the psalmist does with the turn. He does not deny the sorrow. He sets beside it what he knows: God's loving devotion, his hesed, the love that keeps its promises. Pray the whole psalm, all six verses. If you cannot yet say verse 5 for yourself, say it as the church's words, and let them wait in you until they become your own.
